question: Which virulence factor of Helicobacter pylori directly enables its survival in the acidic gastric lumen by creating a protective alkaline microenvironment?

answers.text: Urease — hydrolyses urea into ammonia and CO₂, raising local pH around the bacterium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. H. pylori produces powerful urease that splits urea → NH₃ + CO₂. The ammonia creates an alkaline cloud neutralising gastric acid locally. This enzyme is so characteristic that nearly every diagnostic test (CLO test, urea breath test, stool antigen) exploits its activity.

answers.text: CagA — injected into epithelial cells via a type IV secretion system

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CagA is an oncoprotein injected into host cells that activates Ras–ERK signalling and increases cancer risk. It does not protect the bacterium from gastric acid — that role belongs to urease.

answers.text: VacA — induces vacuolation and apoptosis in gastric epithelial cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: VacA damages epithelial cells contributing to ulceration, but does not neutralise acid. The bacterium needs urease-mediated alkalinisation to survive before it can colonise and deploy VacA.

answers.text: Sheathed flagella — enable motility through the viscous gastric mucus layer

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Flagella enable H. pylori to burrow through the mucus layer to reach the epithelial surface, but they do not protect against acid. Urease provides the critical acid-neutralising mechanism that permits colonisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: H. pylori survival: urease → urea → NH₃ + CO₂ → alkaline microenvironment → acid neutralisation. This is why CLO test and urea breath test detect urease activity.
Urease is the signature enzyme of H. pylori — both a survival mechanism and the basis of most diagnostic tests.
